name: microservices-sprawl
intent: Records what Microservices Sprawl costs: more services, dependencies and operational obligations than the organisation can govern, so the estate stops being changeable — and the price is that the deployment count multiplies every cross-cutting change, the cognitive load per developer exceeds what a team can hold, and the microservices become the legacy they replaced.
problem: Services are added faster than they are consolidated, each one is individually reasonable, and no one is deciding whether the estate is governable. There is no owner, no unit-cost hypothesis, no deprecation path, and every addition multiplies the cost of everything that is not local to one service.
context: The clearest framing is that sprawl is not 'too many services' but unmanaged growth in services, dependencies and operational obligations relative to the organisation's ability to govern them. That distinction matters because the operational tax of microservices is proportional to the service count: updating a shared library means updating it in every repository, a framework upgrade means running every pipeline, and a cross-cutting concern such as a log format change, an authentication update or an error handling convention means touching every service, where in a monolith each was a single change. Microservices.io states the decomposition rule directly: a better approach is to start with one service per team, since that is the bare minimum needed for teams to be loosely coupled, and additional services should only be defined when doing so clearly solves a problem with maintainability or testability. The Premature Microservices case adds the operational half: without centralised logging, distributed tracing, automated service discovery and container orchestration, a team that adopts microservices before building that foundation is in a worse position than with the monolith, which was at least observable.
benefits: It is diagnosable from the numbers rather than from opinion: services that are always deployed together, services with no owner, cross-service changes, and time spent on service infrastructure rather than features.
It separates sprawl from 'too many services', which makes the remedy actionable — the question is governability, not count.

The governance answer is specific and cheap: no production service without an owner, an on-call policy and a runbook; no new service without a cost attribution tag and a unit-cost hypothesis; no public API without versioning and deprecation dates.
It is reversible in a way a bad architecture decision usually is not: merging two services that always deploy together is a course correction based on evidence, not a failure.
It has a named consolidation technique — find the clusters of services that always call each other using tracing data, and merge those first.
tradeoffs: The consolidation is real work and the strongest teams are the ones who can least afford it, which is why sprawl is usually recognised too late to fix cheaply.

Autonomy needs constraints. Freedom without standards becomes chaos, and modern practice moves those standards into platforms, templates and policy controls — which is an investment that also has to be funded.

The observable symptoms are social as well as technical: a common complaint is that everything works fine until another team has to be engaged, and a hypothetical comparison of two squads with identical throughput finds one spending 70% of its effort coordinating upstream and downstream dependencies.

Not every over-decomposition is sprawl. A team of 50 with 60 well-bounded services owned by autonomous teams may be governable; the criterion is governance capacity, which is why the count alone is the wrong metric.
Consolidation destroys some real benefits. A merged service loses its independent deployment and independent scaling, so a merge is a deliberate trade and not a free win.
The platform answer can become its own sprawl: 55.9% of companies run more than one platform, and controlled plurality requires its own governance.
quality_attributes_note: Scores describe the system while the smell is present. Observability is the lowest axis and for a specific reason: sprawl is what makes a system undiagnosable — a latency spike in one service causes timeouts in three others, and the investigation that was one stack trace becomes cross-process correlation. Extensibility and coupling are both bad because the same changes that should be local become fleet-wide. Reliability is mid rather than low because the services individually work; the failures are in the interactions, which is exactly where the missing tracing hides them.

participants.responsibility: One unit in the catalogue, which must be owned, deployed, versioned, observed and eventually retired.
participants.notes: A service exists to be independently changed and deployed; if it is always deployed with another, it is a module.

participants.responsibility: The owner of a service, whose autonomy is the entire benefit being pursued and whose coordination cost is the entire cost being paid.
participants.notes: The decomposition rule is one service per team as the bare minimum; more requires more teams.

participants.responsibility: The catalogue of services, dependencies, pipelines, environments and contracts, which must be governable for the pattern to pay off.
participants.notes: Sprawl is defined by the gap between the estate's growth and the organisation's ability to govern it.

use_cases: Adding a service for every technical layer: AuthService, ValidationService, LoggingService, MetricsService, NotificationService, HealthCheckService, alongside the real business services.
A create-order flow crossing eight services where the domain needed two.
Services that have never been deployed independently of each other, which are modules sharing a deployment.
A team of ten maintaining a dozen repositories, pipelines and service-mesh configurations, spending more time on service infrastructure than on features.
Several teams operating several platforms with inconsistent pipelines, duplicated authentication adapters and uneven logging.
A catalogue with services that have no owner, no on-call policy and no runbook, which is legacy the moment it is created.
avoid_when: There is no scaling bottleneck requiring independent scaling of a specific component, no multiple autonomous teams needing independent deployment, and the monolith's deployment frequency is not limited by size or coupling. If all three answers are no, a modular monolith delivers faster.
The decomposition is one service per team and each service corresponds to a business capability a team can own end to end.
The team can name the specific problem a service solves — maintainability, testability, scaling, an organisational boundary — rather than 'microservices are how you do DevOps'.

The operational foundation exists first: centralised logging, distributed tracing, service discovery or a mesh, container orchestration, health-check-based routing, and a standardised pipeline template new services adopt by default.
The alternative being considered is a big-bang rewrite; a modular monolith with clear internal boundaries and one pipeline is the cheaper step and achieves most of the delivery goal.
Further decomposition is genuinely required and the operational capacity exists — then the count is not the problem and governance is the answer.
pitfalls: Counting services as the metric. Governability is the criterion; a governable estate of 60 is fine and an ungovernable estate of 12 is not.
Identifying bounded contexts with service boundaries, producing 50 services in a domain with 8 contexts — the irony is that DDD advocates larger, cohesive boundaries.
Creating a service per team boundary regardless of whether the boundary makes technical sense, which is organisational Conway's Law run amok.
Continuing to create services while implementing governance, which doubles the backlog and produces the backlog-with-a-backlog.
Treating the sunk cost of the split as a reason to keep it, when the relevant comparison is the ongoing cost of an estate that is slower to change than the monolith it replaced.
Adding a service whose only function is technical (logging, caching, validation, rate limiting) — those are libraries or sidecars of the calling service, not services.
No deprecation path, so services accumulate with their contracts, and every consumer of every retired API remains coupled to it.

related_patterns_notes.module: The consolidation target is a module: services that always deploy together become modules inside one deployable, which keeps the compile-time boundary and removes the deployment boundary. The microservices structure itself is catalogued separately in the architecture catalog as microservices-architecture; this record covers the estate that outgrew its governance, not the structure.
related_patterns_notes.registry: A service catalogue is the primary sprawl countermeasure, and the failure mode to avoid is a centralised catalogue that cannot keep pace with the release rate, which produces shadow wikis and a return to asking around.
related_patterns_notes.gateway: An API gateway concentrates the cross-service surface and is where a cross-cutting change can be made once rather than in every service — the structural mitigation for a change that would otherwise be multiplied by the service count.
related_patterns_notes.bulkhead: A bulkhead per service limits what one service's failure does to the rest, which is both a resilience pattern and the thing that makes fine-grained decomposition survivable at all.
related_patterns_notes.idempotent-receiver: As the service count grows the retry and duplication rate grows with it, and idempotent receivers are what stop a delivery retry from becoming a correctness problem — a requirement that scales with the estate.
related_patterns_notes.scatter-gather: A request that fans out across a dozen nano-services to complete one operation is scatter-gather used for a decision that belonged in one place, and it is both the latency symptom and the cohesion failure of over-decomposition.
related_patterns_notes.anti-corruption-layer: Anti-corruption layers are what make service boundaries negotiable; where they are absent, every consumer is coupled to the provider's model and consolidation becomes impossible.
related_patterns_notes.plugin: A plugin or extension point inside a service is the local answer to a technical function that was promoted to a service: the capability stays close to the code that uses it and does not need its own pipeline.

anti_patterns: The nano-service: a single utility function exposed as a service, so one business operation needs ten network hops and ten failure points.
One service per team boundary regardless of technical sense, creating services so tiny they cannot justify their own existence.
A team maintaining dozens of repositories, pipelines and deployment configurations for an application that handles modest traffic with no component that needs independent scaling.
A cross-cutting change — a log format, an authentication scheme, an error handling convention — meaning one change in every service, where in a monolith it was one change.
Services that have never been deployed independently, which are modules that happen to have their own pipeline.
Adopting microservices without centralised logging, distributed tracing, service discovery and orchestration, leaving a collection of black boxes that cannot be diagnosed.
A catalogue with services that have no owner, no on-call policy and no runbook — legacy from the day they are created.
Several platforms instead of one, with inconsistent pipelines and duplicated authentication adapters, which is the sprawl answer creating more sprawl.
Continuing to add services while implementing governance, doubling the backlog instead of stopping the growth.
design_principles: One service per team as the starting point: that is the bare minimum for teams to be loosely coupled, and additional services must solve a demonstrable problem.
Size the service by business capability, not by technical function, because a service a team can own end to end is the unit that delivers the benefit.
Make the operational tax proportional and known: every service adds a pipeline, monitoring, versioning, documentation and coordination, and that tax is what the count must be justified against.
Own everything in production: no service without an owner, an on-call policy and a runbook; no new service without a cost attribution and a unit-cost hypothesis.
Govern the lifecycle, not only the creation: explicit lifecycle states, versioning and deprecation dates on every public API, and continuous retirement.
Consolidation is a first-class operation: merging services that always deploy together is a course correction based on evidence, and should be as routine as creation.
best_practices: Audit the estate before deciding anything: count services, map services to teams, identify technical-utility services and services that are always deployed together, and produce a consolidation list before adding anything.
Use distributed tracing data to find the clusters: services that call each other in 95% of their operations are candidates for consolidation, and the most coupled cluster is the one to merge first.
Merge services owned by the same team before splitting anything — a single team running six services gets the autonomy benefit from one deployable.
Make ownership mandatory and enforced by the platform: services without an owner cannot pass a gate; this is a simple rule that reduces sprawl quickly.
Require a unit-cost hypothesis and a cost attribution tag for every new service, so the operational tax is stated at creation rather than discovered at year two.
Standardise: paved roads, a pipeline template new services adopt by default, and policy as code, so autonomy has constraints rather than chaos.
Budget the cross-cutting change explicitly: any change that must touch every service needs either a platform-level mechanism or an acknowledged fleet-wide cost.
Make lifecycle states real: a service without a deprecation path is legacy immediately, so retirement must be a scheduled operation with an owner.

Ask the decomposition question before creating a service: is there a current scaling bottleneck (not a theoretical future one), are there multiple autonomous teams, and is the monolith's deployment frequency actually limited by size or coupling?

Treat the migration's business case as measurable: lead time and change fail rate should improve as operational overhead shrinks; if they do not, the sprawl diagnosis is confirmed and consolidation is cheaper than continuing.
sources: Sam Newman, 'Microservices adoption anti-pattern: More the merrier', microservices.io, 2019 — the fine-grained decomposition anti-pattern, the statement that defining more services moves complexity from within the services to between them with diminishing returns, the rule that a better approach is to start with one service per team as the bare minimum needed for loosely coupled teams, and that additional services should be defined only when doing so clearly solves a maintainability or testability problem.

Atlassian, 'How to tame software sprawl' — sprawl defined as the number of applications or components growing and changing rapidly enough that traditional management fails; the symptom of post-incident reviews naming upstream changes as root cause; the worked comparison of two squads with identical throughput where one spends 70% of effort coordinating upstream dependencies; the centralised catalogue with decentralised management as the self-service remedy; and the finding that governance functions become the bottleneck (56% of respondents in the 2022 State of DevOps felt security processes slow delivery).

MinimumCD.org, 'Premature Microservices' — the operational tax is proportional to the number of services (a shared library update is one change in a monolith and N in microservices); without centralised logging, distributed tracing, service discovery and orchestration the architecture is a collection of black boxes; the three diagnostic questions (a current scaling bottleneck, multiple autonomous teams, deployment frequency actually limited by size or coupling); and the merge rule that services that have never been deployed independently are modules.

Maria Hafez, 'Service Sprawl After Microservices: Avoid the New Legacy' — the definition of sprawl as unmanaged growth in services, dependencies and operational obligations relative to the organisation's ability to govern them; the year-two risk framing; portfolio drift where services overlap, business rules are duplicated and data is copied; the governance rules (no production service without an owner, on-call policy and runbook; no new service without a cost attribution tag and a unit cost hypothesis; no public API without versioning and deprecation dates; no shared database writes across services); and the State of Platform Engineering Vol 4 finding that 55.9% of companies operate more than one platform.

Paul Serban, 'Avoiding the Grains of Sand Anti-Pattern in Microservices', 2024 — 200 services where 15 would do; the three causes (misreading 'micro', Conway's Law run amok, bounded contexts mistaken for service boundaries); the startup test ('could this team build a startup around this service') and the rule of threes for data coupling; and the consolidation procedure using tracing data and a service dependency matrix.

ArchMan, 'Nano-services' — the worked example of a 25-service e-commerce platform where create-order crosses eight services at 10ms each; the granularity table (monolith / 20+ nano-services / 5-15 right-sized); and the guidance that services should be coarse-grained, aligned to business capabilities, and split only when clear scaling benefits emerge.
